title: Linux File Operations
description: Master essential file manipulation commands including copy, move, link, search, archive, and transfer operations.

tasks.prompt: In your writable /home/user directory, report.txt is a readable regular file. You own the existing writable directory /home/user/backups, and backups/report.txt does not exist. Use GNU cp to copy report.txt there without changing its filename or moving the original.
tasks.hint: Pass cp the source file and existing destination directory: cp report.txt /home/user/backups/
tasks.explanation: cp reads the source and creates a separate copy at the destination. When the destination is an existing directory, it retains the source basename. Both locations are accessible to you, so sudo is unnecessary.

tasks.prompt: In your writable /home/user directory, draft.txt is a regular file you own and final.txt does not exist. Use GNU mv to rename draft.txt to final.txt here.
tasks.hint: Give mv the current name followed by the new name: mv draft.txt final.txt
tasks.explanation: mv changes the name at the destination. Since both paths are in the same directory, this is a rename. Unlike cp, it leaves no separate draft.txt copy.

tasks.prompt: In your writable /home/user directory, notes.txt may be absent or may be a regular file you own. Use GNU touch to create an empty file if absent; otherwise update both its access and modification timestamps to the current time without changing its contents.
tasks.hint: Use touch with no timestamp-selection flags: touch notes.txt
tasks.explanation: touch creates an empty file if necessary and updates access and modification times by default. It does not truncate existing contents. -c would prevent creation; -a or -m alone would update only one timestamp.

tasks.prompt: You are in your writable /home/user directory and config_link does not exist. /etc/nginx/nginx.conf is an existing regular file. Use GNU ln to create a symbolic link named config_link here that points to that absolute path.
tasks.hint: Put the target before the new link name: ln -s /etc/nginx/nginx.conf config_link
tasks.explanation: ln -s creates a symbolic link whose contents identify the target path. The new link is created in your writable directory; creating it does not change nginx.conf and does not need sudo. Without -s, ln would attempt a hard link.

tasks.prompt: On this host, you can read and search the entire /var directory tree. Use GNU find to print the paths of regular files named exactly error.log, matching case; exclude directories with that name.
tasks.hint: Combine the regular-file and exact-name tests: find /var -type f -name 'error.log'
tasks.explanation: find walks the directory tree. -type f limits matches to regular files; -name checks the basename with case-sensitive shell-pattern matching. The exact error.log pattern contains no wildcard. Matches are printed by default.

tasks.prompt: In your writable /home/user directory, you own and can read/search project and all its contents. GNU tar and gzip are available; project.tar.gz does not exist. Use tar to create that gzip-compressed archive containing the project directory and its contents, leaving the originals in place.
tasks.hint: Use create, gzip, and archive-file options: tar -czf project.tar.gz project
tasks.explanation: tar -c creates an archive, -z compresses it with gzip, and -f names the archive file. The project directory remains intact. Merely choosing a .gz filename without compression does not gzip an archive; -a is also valid here because it selects compression from the .gz suffix.

tasks.prompt: In your writable /home/user directory, data.csv is a readable regular file you own, with one hard link; data.csv.gz does not exist. GNU gzip is available. Compress data.csv in place into data.csv.gz, removing the uncompressed original after success.
tasks.hint: gzip replaces the named input file by default: gzip data.csv
tasks.explanation: gzip normally replaces a regular input file with its compressed .gz form after successful compression. -k keeps the original, contrary to this goal; -c writes compressed bytes to stdout instead of creating data.csv.gz. Compression-level options such as -9 remain valid.

tasks.prompt: In /home/user, rsync is installed and src/ and dest/ are existing directories you own. All src contents are readable regular files, directories, or symlinks you own; you can preserve their groups and write to dest. Use rsync in archive mode to copy the contents of src into dest, preserving attributes and symlinks. Keep destination-only files.
tasks.hint: Use archive mode and a trailing slash on the source: rsync -a src/ dest/
tasks.explanation: rsync -a enables recursive copying with archive attributes, including permissions, timestamps, and symlinks. The source trailing slash copies its contents directly into dest rather than creating dest/src. Archive mode does not delete destination-only files; --delete would change that behavior.
